 Under the Skin Netflix Departure: Scarlett Johansson’s Unsettling Sci-Fi Masterpiece Leaves Streaming This Halloween
 Home 
 Society 
 Felix Yim 
 2 hours 47 minutes ago
 One of the most divisive and mesmerizing science fiction films of the 21st century is about to disappear from Netflix. Jonathan Glazer’s Under the Skin , starring Scarlett Johansson as an alien predator stalking men across Scotland, will officially leave the streaming platform on October 31, 2026.
 The departure coincides with Halloween weekend, offering subscribers a final, fleeting chance to experience a film that captivated critics but confounded mainstream audiences upon its release more than a decade ago.
 The Final Countdown: Why Under the Skin Is Leaving Netflix Now
 Netflix’s licensing agreements are notoriously fluid, and Under the Skin is the latest casualty of the platform’s rotating catalog. The film arrived on Netflix in May 2026, finding a new generation of viewers and even climbing to No. 10 on Moviefone’s Netflix streaming chart. However, that window is closing. As of October 31, 2026, the film will no longer be available to stream on the platform, meaning subscribers have just days to watch or re-watch Glazer’s haunting vision before it vanishes into the licensing ether.
 The timing is particularly poignant. Under the Skin is not a traditional horror film, but its creeping dread, unsettling imagery, and predatory protagonist make it an ideal—if deeply unconventional—Halloween watch. Its departure on the holiday itself feels like a cruel trick from the streaming gods, removing a genuinely singular cinematic experience at the exact moment audiences might be most receptive to its eerie atmosphere.
 A Predator in Plain Sight: The Story That Defies Genre
 To understand why the film’s departure matters, one must revisit what makes Under the Skin so extraordinary. Based on Michel Faber’s 2000 novel, the film follows an extraterrestrial organism that assumes the form of a beautiful woman (Johansson) and roams the bleak, rain-soaked landscapes of Scotland. She picks up men—often lonely, vulnerable, or simply unsuspecting—and lures them back to a nondescript house. There, they are submerged into an inky, infinite void, their bodies harvested for reasons the film never fully explains.
 What begins as a familiar alien-invasion premise morphs into something far stranger and more profound. As the woman interacts with her victims and observes the world around her, she begins to develop a fragmented understanding of human empathy, vulnerability, and mortality. The film becomes a meditation on what it means to be human, filtered through the eyes of a being that is fundamentally inhuman. It is a slow-burn, almost experimental piece of filmmaking that prioritizes atmosphere and sensory experience over conventional narrative. Johansson’s performance is largely silent, relying on physicality and an uncanny stillness that makes her character both alluring and deeply alien.
 The Critical Divide: A Masterpiece or an Experiment?
 Under the Skin is a film that demands patience and rewards contemplation, but it is not for everyone. Upon its release, it garnered near-universal praise from critics, earning an 84% score on Rotten Tomatoes and a BAFTA nomination for Outstanding British Film. It has since been cited on numerous lists of the best films of the 21st century, celebrated for its audacious vision and Glazer’s uncompromising direction.
 Yet, the audience score on Rotten Tomatoes sits at a starkly lower 55%, highlighting the profound disconnect between critical acclaim and mainstream accessibility. Many viewers found the film’s glacial pacing, lack of exposition, and abstract imagery frustrating. Its commercial performance reflected this divide: it grossed just $7.4 million against a production budget exceeding $13 million, a significant box office disappointment for a film starring an A-list actress at the height of her fame. For those willing to surrender to its rhythm, however, Under the Skin offers a uniquely hypnotic and disturbing experience that lingers long after the credits roll.
 Where to Watch After the Netflix Departure
 For subscribers who miss the October 31 deadline—or for those who wish to revisit the film without a Netflix subscription—there are still options. Under the Skin remains available to rent or purchase on digital platforms, but for those seeking a free, ad-supported option, several services may carry the film. Viewers in the United States can check platforms like Tubi, Roku, Pluto TV, and Fandango, though availability varies by region and may change at any time. Physical media collectors can also seek out the Blu-ray or DVD, which often includes bonus features and commentary tracks that deepen the appreciation of Glazer’s meticulous craft.
 A New Skin: The Looming Television Adaptation
 The film’s departure from Netflix is not the end of the Under the Skin story. In a fascinating twist, the property is being reimagined for television. Silver Reel, the production company that originally financed Glazer’s film, won a heated bidding war against A24 for the rights to create a TV spin-off. The series is expected to draw from Faber’s novel while remaining “very respectful” of Glazer’s cinematic vision, though specific plot details and a release date remain under wraps.
 This development adds a layer of intrigue to the film’s streaming departure. While the original movie leaves Netflix, the universe it created is poised to expand into a new medium, potentially introducing the story to an even broader audience. Whether the series can capture the enigmatic, visceral power of the film remains to be seen, but it ensures that Under the Skin will continue to provoke and unsettle for years to come.
 Why You Should Watch Before It’s Gone
 Under the Skin is not a comfortable watch, but it is an essential one for anyone interested in the outer limits of science fiction and the art of filmmaking. It is a film that trusts its audience to sit with ambiguity, to find meaning in silence and imagery, and to confront the uncomfortable proximity between the alien and the intimately human. With its departure from Netflix imminent, now is the time to experience—or revisit—a work that continues to divide, haunt, and fascinate in equal measure. After October 31, you will have to look a little harder to find it, but the film’s haunting impression will remain long after the screen goes dark.
